learn: k-NN for classification and regression; distance-weighted k-NN
Dissimilarity measures: data and dissimilarity matrices, nominal, binary (symmetric/asymmetric, Jaccard), Minkowski family, standardisation, ordinal, Gower
Curse of dimensionality and choosing k
Locally weighted (linear) regression with kernel-weighted gradient descent
Model selection: train/validation/test, holdout, k-fold, stratified and leave-one-out cross-validation
intro.why: Distance-based reasoning underlies k-NN, kernel methods, clustering (Module 10), recommender systems and vector search. The evaluation protocol in the second half applies to every model.

sections.title: Instance-based vs model-based learning
sections.plain: Store and compare, or fit and discard.
sections.body:
Instance-based: compare new points to known points; lazy learners spend less time training and more predicting. Model-based: detect patterns and build a predictive model; eager learners spend more time training and less predicting.

Model-based: use $X$ and $y$ to learn $\theta_0..\theta_n$, giving $f(x)=\theta_0x_0+\dots+\theta_nx_n$, which predicts new inputs (e.g. $f(x_i)=39$, $f(x_j)=1$). Instance-based: store the data; for a query $y_i=?$ search for similar stored points (e.g. $x_4,x_9,x_{15}$) and use them: $\hat y_i=\frac{y_4+y_9+y_{15}}{3}$.

sections.title: The nearest-neighbour approach
sections.plain: Vote for classes, average for numbers.
sections.body:
Basic idea: compute the distance from the test record to all training records, choose the $k$ nearest, and use their labels. Notation: given $x_q$, take a vote among its $k$ nearest neighbours for a discrete target, or the mean (or median) for a real-valued target, $\hat f(x_q)=\frac1k\sum_{i=1}^kf(x_i)$. Instances are points in Euclidean space; the 15 white/pink points illustrate.

k-NN regression: house size → price; 3-NN for a query gives $(50+55+51)/3=52$, with $d(x_i,x_j)=\sqrt{\sum_{r=1}^n(a_r(x_i)-a_r(x_j))^2}$.

sections.title: Data and dissimilarity matrices
sections.plain: n × p data; n × n lower-triangular distances.
sections.body: Data matrix: $n$ points × $p$ dimensions, entries $x_{if}$. Dissimilarity matrix: $n\times n$, records only distances; triangular because $d(i,j)=d(j,i)$ and $d(i,i)=0$.

sections.title: Nominal attributes
sections.plain: Share of mismatches, or one-hot.
sections.body: Nominal attributes take 2 or more states (red, yellow, blue, green). Method 1, simple matching: $d(i,j)=\frac{p-m}{p}$, $m$ = number of matches, $p$ = number of variables. Method 2: create a binary attribute for each of the $M$ states (one-hot).

sections.title: Binary attributes and Jaccard
sections.plain: Ignore 0-0 matches for asymmetric attributes.
sections.body:
Contingency table: $q$ = both 1, $r$ = $i$ 1 / $j$ 0, $s$ = $i$ 0 / $j$ 1, $t$ = both 0, $p=q+r+s+t$.

$$d_{sym}(i,j)=\frac{r+s}{q+r+s+t},\qquad d_{asym}(i,j)=\frac{r+s}{q+r+s},\qquad \text{sim}_{Jaccard}(i,j)=\frac{q}{q+r+s}.$$

Example: Jack, Mary, Jim with gender (symmetric, excluded) and Fever, Cough, Test-1..4 (asymmetric; Y/P = 1, N = 0): $$d(\text{jack},\text{mary})=\frac{0+1}{2+0+1}=0.33,\quad d(\text{jack},\text{jim})=\frac{1+1}{1+1+1}=0.67,\quad d(\text{jim},\text{mary})=\frac{1+2}{1+1+2}=0.75.$$ Jack and Mary are most likely to have a similar disease.

sections.title: Minkowski distance and its special cases
sections.plain: L_h norm of the difference.
sections.body:
$$d(i,j)=\sqrt[h]{|x_{i1}-x_{j1}|^h+|x_{i2}-x_{j2}|^h+\dots+|x_{ip}-x_{jp}|^h}\quad(L_h\text{ norm}).$$

Metric properties: $d(i,j)>0$ if $i\ne j$ and $d(i,i)=0$ (positive definiteness); $d(i,j)=d(j,i)$ (symmetry); $d(i,j)\le d(i,k)+d(k,j)$ (triangle inequality). Special cases: $h=1$ Manhattan ($L_1$; Hamming distance for bit vectors), $h=2$ Euclidean ($L_2$), $h\to\infty$ supremum ($L_{\max}$/$L_\infty$): $d(i,j)=\lim_{h\to\infty}\left(\sum_f|x_{if}-x_{jf}|^h\right)^{1/h}=\max_f|x_{if}-x_{jf}|$.

Example, points $x_1=(1,2)$, $x_2=(3,5)$, $x_3=(2,0)$, $x_4=(4,5)$:

sections.title: Standardising numeric data; ordinal variables
sections.plain: z-scores for numbers; rank then scale for ordinals.
sections.body: Z-score: $z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$, the distance from the mean in standard deviations (negative below the mean). Ordinal variables: replace $x_{if}$ by its rank $r_{if}\in\{1,\dots,M_f\}$, then map to [0, 1]: $z_{if}=\frac{r_{if}-1}{M_f-1}$, and treat as interval-scaled.

sections.title: Mixed attribute types: Gower distance
sections.plain: Average of per-column dissimilarities in [0, 1].
sections.body:
$$d(i,j)=\frac{\sum_{c=1}^{n}w_c\,\delta_{ij}^{(c)}d_{ij}^{(c)}}{\sum_{c=1}^{n}w_c\,\delta_{ij}^{(c)}}$$

$\delta_{ij}^{(c)}=0$ if column $c$ is missing for $i$ or $j$, or if it is asymmetric binary and both are 0; else 1. Categorical: $d^{(c)}_{ij}=0$ if equal, else 1. Continuous/ordinal: $d^{(c)}_{ij}=\frac{|x_{ic}-x_{jc}|}{\max_c-\min_c}$.

Example: Ram (70,000, Doctor, Bengali, Village), Balram (50,000, Data Scientist, Hindi, Small Town), Bharat (60,000, Carpenter, Hindi, Suburban), Kishan (80,000, Doctor, Bhojpuri, Metropolitan). After min-max income (0.67, 0, 0.33, 1) and ranks 1–4: sums d(Ram, Balram) = 3, d(Ram, Bharat) = 3, d(Ram, Kishan) = 2.33, d(Balram, Bharat) = 1.67, d(Balram, Kishan) = 3.67, d(Bharat, Kishan) = 3. Gower = sum/4 (0 to 1). Most similar: Balram–Bharat; most dissimilar: Balram–Kishan.

sections.title: Curse of dimensionality
sections.plain: Irrelevant attributes swamp the distance.
sections.body:
k-NN uses all attributes. If the target depends on only a few of many attributes, truly similar instances may be far apart. Nearest neighbour is easily misled in high dimensions. Solution 1: weight attributes (stretch relevant axes, shrink irrelevant ones), choosing weights by cross-validation. Solution 2: eliminate the least relevant attributes, again by cross-validation.

Supplementary For random points in $d$ dimensions, $\frac{d_{\max}-d_{\min}}{d_{\min}}\to0$ as $d$ grows: all points become nearly equidistant.

sections.title: The k-NN algorithm
sections.plain: Store; at query time find k nearest and vote or average.
sections.body:
TRAINING:   for each example ⟨x, f(x)⟩: add it to training_examples

CLASSIFY(x_q):                       # discrete f: ℜⁿ → V
  x₁..x_k ← k instances of training_examples nearest to x_q
  return argmax_{v∈V} Σᵢ δ(v, f(xᵢ))

REGRESS(x_q):                        # real-valued f: ℜⁿ → ℜ
  return (1/k) Σᵢ f(xᵢ)

Supplementary Brute force costs $O(nd)$ per query and $O(nd)$ memory; kd-trees reduce queries to about $O(\log n)$ in low dimensions.

sections.title: Choosing k: rule of thumb and elbow method
sections.plain: √N as a start; validate and pick the elbow.
sections.body: Rule of thumb: $k=\sqrt N$, $N$ = number of training points. Elbow method: compute SSE (or any error) for $k=1..X$ on validation data; pick $k$ where the curve flattens. Note: as $k$ approaches the total number of instances, the error on training data does not simply decrease; the statement that it "drops to 0" should be read as $k=1$ giving zero training error.

sections.title: Distance-weighted k-NN
sections.plain: Weight votes by 1/d² or a kernel.
sections.body:
$$\text{discrete: }\hat f(x_q)\leftarrow\arg\max_{v\in V}\sum_{i=1}^kw_i\,\delta(v,f(x_i)),\qquad w_i\equiv\frac1{d(x_q,x_i)}\ \text{(a commonly quoted version uses }1/d^2),\ \hat f(x_q)=f(x_i)\text{ if }x_q=x_i$$ $$\text{continuous: }\hat f(x_q)\leftarrow\frac{\sum_{i=1}^kw_if(x_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^kw_i}$$

Kernel functions $w_i=K(d(x_q,x_i))$: $1/d^2$; $1/(d_0+d)^2$; $\exp(-(d/\sigma_0)^2)$.

sections.title: Problem type 1: changing k
sections.plain: The class at (1,1) flips as k grows.
sections.body:
Points X1 (−1, 1) N, X2 (0, 1) P, X3 (0, 2) N, X4 (1, −1) N, X5 (1, 0) P, X6 (1, 2) P, X7 (2, 2) N, X8 (2, 3) P. Distances from (1, 1): X2, X5, X6 = 1; X3, X7 = 1.414; X1, X4 = 2; X8 = 2.236.

  • $k=3$: X2, X5, X6 → 3 P → Positive.
  • $k=5$: + X3, X7 (N) → 3 P, 2 N → Positive.
  • $k=7$: + X1, X4 (N) → 3 P, 4 N → Negative.

Combining k = 3, 5, 7 by majority gives Positive (2 of 3).

sections.title: Locally weighted (linear) regression
sections.plain: Fit a kernel-weighted line around each query.
sections.body:
Local: approximated from data near the query; weighted: each example's contribution depends on its distance; regression: real-valued target. Residual $\hat f(x)-f(x)$; kernel $w_i=K(d(x_i,x_q))$. Nearest-neighbour methods approximate $f$ at a single point; LWR builds an explicit local approximation (linear, quadratic, a small NN…) over a neighbourhood.

Local linear model $\hat f(x)=w_0+w_1a_1(x)+\dots+w_na_n(x)$ fitted by gradient descent with a redefined error:

$$E_1(x_q)=\tfrac12\sum_{x\in kNN(x_q)}(f(x)-\hat f(x))^2,\quad E_2(x_q)=\tfrac12\sum_{x\in D}(f(x)-\hat f(x))^2K(d(x_q,x)),\quad E_3(x_q)=\tfrac12\sum_{x\in kNN(x_q)}(f(x)-\hat f(x))^2K(d(x_q,x)).$$

Gradient rule for $E_3$: $$\Delta w_j=\eta\sum_{x\in kNN(x_q)}K(d(x_q,x))\,(f(x)-\hat f(x))\,a_j(x),\qquad w_j\leftarrow w_j+\Delta w_j.$$ A new regression problem is solved for every query; ordinary linear regression solves one problem globally.

sections.plain: 5-NN, Gaussian kernel, one update: prediction 9.1 → 6.46.

sections.title: When to use nearest neighbours
sections.plain: Low dimensions, lots of data, complex targets.
sections.body:
• Low-dimensional data.
  • Local information yields highly adaptive behaviour.
  • Lots of training data (distance-weighted k-NN): training is very fast; complex targets can be learned; no information is lost.
  • Noisy data (distance-weighted k-NN): averaging the k nearest smooths out isolated noisy examples.

sections.title: Challenges of nearest-neighbour classifiers
sections.plain: Choosing k and the metric; slow queries; memory.
sections.body:
• The value of $k$.
  • The distance metric.
  • Expensive at query time: distance to all $N$ examples. Remedies: pre-sort into fast structures (kd-trees), remove redundant data (condensing).
  • Storage: all training data must be kept; remedy: condensing.

sections.title: Model selection and assessment; hyperparameter tuning
sections.plain: Tune on validation; assess once on test.
sections.body:
Model selection: estimate performance of models to choose one. Model assessment: estimate the chosen model's generalisation error on new data. Split into a training set (fit), validation set (model selection, hyperparameters, feature selection) and test set (final assessment).

Tuning on the test set fails: comparing linear vs polynomial models on the test set, or trying 100 regularisation values and choosing the one with the lowest test error (5%), leads to 15% errors in production, because the model and hyperparameters were adapted to that particular test set. The test data can't be used for parameter tuning.

Holdout validation: train models with various hyperparameters on the reduced training set; select the best on the validation set; retrain it on the full training set (incl. validation); evaluate once on the test set.

sections.title: Cross-validation
sections.plain: Rotate the validation fold and average.
sections.body:
Don't touch the test set until confident. A small validation set gives imprecise evaluations; a large one leaves little training data. Solution: cross-validation: split the training data into $k$ folds; for each split, train on $k-1$ folds and validate on the remaining one; average the $k$ metrics; then retrain on all training data and evaluate on the test set.

Techniques: holdout; k-fold; stratified k-fold (preserves class proportions per fold); leave-one-out (k = n). For hyperparameter tuning: for each parameter combination compute the cross-validated metric, choose the best, retrain on all training data, compute the test metric.

scikit-learn: scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=10); avg = np.mean(scores). Typical train/test split 80/20; a single split wastes labelled data.

sections.title: Complexity, comparisons and misconceptions
sections.body:
k-NNLogistic regressionDecision tree
Training cost$O(1)$ (store)$O(nd)$ per iteration$O(nd\log n)$
Prediction cost$O(nd)$ brute force$O(d)$$O(\text{depth})$
MemoryAll data$O(d)$Tree size
Needs scalingYesFor GD/regularisationNo
BoundaryArbitrary (Voronoi)LinearAxis-aligned
  • "1-NN is useless." Asymptotically its error is at most twice the Bayes error (Cover–Hart).
  • "Cross-validation estimates the final model's error exactly." It estimates the expected error of the procedure; nested CV is needed when tuning and assessing together.
  • "LOOCV is always best." Low bias but high variance and cost; 5- or 10-fold is the usual compromise.
  • "Ties don't matter." Use odd $k$ for two classes or distance weighting to break ties.

code.title: k-NN by hand, Minkowski matrices and binary dissimilarity
code.explain: Reproduces problem type 1 (k = 3, 5, 7), the L1/L2/L∞ matrices and the patient dissimilarities.
mistakes: Breaking distance ties arbitrarily without noticing (X2, X5, X6 are all at distance 1).
code.notes: np.argsort(kind='stable') keeps the original order for ties.
code.code:
import numpy as np

# Problem type 1: classify (1, 1) with k = 3, 5, 7
P = np.array([[-1, 1], [0, 1], [0, 2], [1, -1], [1, 0], [1, 2], [2, 2], [2, 3]])
cls = np.array(["Neg", "Pos", "Neg", "Neg", "Pos", "Pos", "Neg", "Pos"])
d = np.linalg.norm(P - [1, 1], axis=1); order = np.argsort(d, kind="stable")
print("distances:", dict(zip([f"X{i+1}" for i in range(8)], d.round(3))))
for k in (3, 5, 7):
    nn = cls[order[:k]]; print(f"k={k}: neighbours {list(nn)} -> {max(set(nn), key=list(nn).count)}")

# Minkowski dissimilarity matrices 
X = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 5], [2, 0], [4, 5]])
for name, h in [("Manhattan L1", 1), ("Euclidean L2", 2), ("Supremum Linf", np.inf)]:
    D = np.array([[np.linalg.norm(a - b, ord=h) for b in X] for a in X])
    print(name); print(np.tril(D).round(2))

# Asymmetric binary dissimilarity: Y/P = 1, N = 0; gender excluded
rows = {"Jack": [1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0], "Mary": [1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0], "Jim": [1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0]}
def d_asym(a, b):
    a, b = np.array(a), np.array(b); q = np.sum((a == 1) & (b == 1)); r = np.sum((a == 1) & (b == 0)); s = np.sum((a == 0) & (b == 1))
    return round((r + s) / (q + r + s), 2)
print("d(jack,mary)", d_asym(rows["Jack"], rows["Mary"]), "d(jack,jim)", d_asym(rows["Jack"], rows["Jim"]), "d(jim,mary)", d_asym(rows["Jim"], rows["Mary"]))

code.title: Locally weighted regression: one gradient step
code.explain: Problem type 3: 5-NN with a Gaussian kernel and one gradient update from y = 3.5 + 0.8x; prediction goes from 9.1 to 6.46.
mistakes: Using all points instead of the k nearest when the problem says 5-NN (that is E2, not E3).
code.notes: Repeating to convergence gives the local weighted least-squares fit.
code.code:
import numpy as np

# Problem type 3: predict price for size 7, 5-NN, kernel exp(-d^2/2b^2), b=1, y = 3.5 + 0.8x, lr 0.2, one iteration
size = np.array([10, 5, 2, 3, 5, 15, 30, 20, 6, 2, 10, 13]); price = np.array([5, 5, 2, 3, 5, 5, 9, 8, 9, 3, 9, 8])
xq, k, lr = 7, 5, 0.2
d = np.abs(size - xq); K = np.exp(-d ** 2 / 2)
nn = np.argsort(d, kind="stable")[:k]
print("5 nearest (size, price, d, K):", [(int(size[i]), int(price[i]), int(d[i]), round(float(K[i]), 3)) for i in nn])
w0, w1 = 3.5, 0.8
err = price[nn] - (w0 + w1 * size[nn])                       # f(x) - f^(x)
w0n = w0 + lr * np.sum(K[nn] * err * 1); w1n = w1 + lr * np.sum(K[nn] * err * size[nn])
print("before: prediction", w0 + w1 * xq)
print(f"after one iteration: w0 = {w0n:.3f}, w1 = {w1n:.3f}, prediction {w0n + w1n * xq:.3f}")

# Plain k-NN regression and distance-weighted k-NN for comparison
print("5-NN mean:", price[nn].mean(), " kernel-weighted 5-NN:", round(float(np.sum(K[nn] * price[nn]) / np.sum(K[nn])), 3))

code.title: Tuning k with cross-validation, with and without scaling
code.explain: Grid-searches k and weighting with stratified 5-fold CV, then reports the untouched test accuracy.
mistakes: Scaling outside the pipeline (leaks fold statistics).
code.notes: Scaling raises test accuracy from 0.90 to 0.96 here.
code.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score, GridSearchCV, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import numpy as np

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=0)
print("rule of thumb k = sqrt(N) =", round(np.sqrt(len(X_tr))))
cv = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
for scale in (False, True):
    knn = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier()) if scale else KNeighborsClassifier()
    grid = GridSearchCV(knn, {"kneighborsclassifier__n_neighbors" if scale else "n_neighbors": [1, 3, 5, 9, 15, 21], 
                              "kneighborsclassifier__weights" if scale else "weights": ["uniform", "distance"]}, cv=cv).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(("scaled  " if scale else "unscaled"), "best", grid.best_params_, "CV acc", round(grid.best_score_, 3), "test acc", round(grid.score(X_te, y_te), 3))
